summary: Agur trusts God’s refined word and asks for two things: freedom from falsehood, and neither poverty nor riches.

context.title: Agur’s prayer for enough
paragraphs: These verses belong to the words of Agur son of Jakeh, an appendix to the proverbs of Solomon. [c1] Some Jewish and Christian interpreters took Agur for Solomon himself, but Ellicott and Poole judge him a separate sage, and Ellicott calls him otherwise unknown. [c2] His sayings open with a confession of how little he knows of God. [c3]

Verse 5 depends closely on Psalm 18:31, and verse 6 on the warning of Deut 4:2 against adding to God’s words. [c4] The name for God here, Eloah, occurs nowhere else in Proverbs, though it is the usual name in Job. [c5] The prayer that follows is the first of Agur’s numerical sayings, built on the number two. [c6]

Agur asks two things before he dies: to be kept from falsehood, and to be spared both poverty and riches. [c7] He gives the reason himself: plenty can breed a proud denial of God, and want can push a person to steal. [c8] The two requests belong together, the first against the sins themselves and the second against their occasions. [c9]

translationNotes.summary: The Hebrew is a smelter’s word: God’s speech is like metal refined in the furnace.
translationNotes.body: The verb behind ṣĕrûpâ means to smelt or refine metal, and from there to test. [c10] Psalm 12:7 uses the same word of silver refined in a furnace, the picture Agur’s line assumes. [c11] The Greek translators rendered it as tried in the fire. [c12] The point is less that God’s word passes an examination than that it holds no dross: it has proved true in use. [c13]

translationNotes.summary: Šāwĕʾ means emptiness or worthlessness; the lie it is paired with is that emptiness spoken aloud.
translationNotes.body: Šāwĕʾ first means emptiness or nothingness, and the lexicon files this verse under empty speech paired with lying. [c14] The Pulpit Commentary reads the pair as inward hollowness and its outward expression in words. [c15] The same noun stands in the commandment against taking up God’s name in vain, Ex 20:7, a name Agur fears to wrong in verse 9. [c16]

translationNotes.summary: Literally “the bread of my portion”: food allotted, like a fixed ration, neither more nor less.
translationNotes.body: Ḥōq means something prescribed, and the lexicon lists this verse under a prescribed portion or allowance of food. [c17] The same noun names the fixed allowance of the Egyptian priests in Gen 47:22. [c18] Agur asks for neither surplus nor scarcity, only what is apportioned to him. [c19] Christian readers hear the daily bread of the Lord’s Prayer, though the Pulpit Commentary notes that the idea is not the same. [c20]

original.gloss: and I lay hold of the name of my God

translationNotes.summary: The verb tāpaś means to seize or handle roughly: want might drive Agur to lay violent hands on God’s name.
translationNotes.body: Tāpaś means to lay hold of or seize, and the lexicon glosses this verse as doing violence to the name of God. [c21] It is not the verb of the commandment about the name, but one of rough seizing. [c22] The Pulpit Commentary reads it either of a false oath sworn to cover a theft, or of bitter complaint against God’s providence in hardship. [c23]

claims.text: Proverbs 30 begins the words of Agur son of Jakeh, part of the appendices that follow the proverbs of Solomon.
Some Jewish writers (Rashi, Gersonides) and some Christian writers identified Agur with Solomon, while Ellicott and Poole judge him to be a different sage, whom Ellicott calls otherwise unknown.
In Prv 30:2-3 Agur acknowledges his own ignorance.
Prv 30:5 depends on Psalm 18:31 (2 Sam 22:31), and Prv 30:6 on Deut 4:2.
The divine name Eloah (אֱלוֹהַּ) in Prv 30:5 occurs nowhere else in Proverbs, while in Job it is the prevailing name of God.
Prv 30:7-9 is the first of Agur’s numerical proverbs.
Agur’s two requests are to be kept from falsehood and from the extremes of poverty and riches.
Prv 30:9 gives the reason: wealth tempts to pride and denial of God, poverty to theft.
The first petition is against the sins themselves, the second against the occasions of them.
The verb צָרַף means to smelt, refine or test.
Psalm 12:7 uses the same Hebrew word of silver refined in a furnace.
The Septuagint renders the line as the words of God being tried in the fire.
God’s word is called pure in the sense of tested and proved, free from falsehood and error.
שָׁוְא means emptiness, nothingness or vanity, and in Prv 30:8 it is empty speech paired with lying.
The Pulpit Commentary takes שָׁוְא as inward hollowness and worthlessness, and the lies as its expression in words.
Exodus 20:7 uses שָׁוְא in the commandment against taking up the name of God in vain, and Prv 30:9 also concerns the name of God.
חֹק means something prescribed, and in Prv 30:8 a prescribed portion or allowance of food.
Gen 47:22 uses חֹק of the portion assigned for the support of the Egyptian priests.
Agur asks for the food apportioned to him as suitable.
Interpreters compare the request with the daily bread of the Lord’s Prayer (Mt 6:11), though the Pulpit Commentary holds that the idea is not the same.
תָּפַשׂ means to lay hold of or seize, and in Prv 30:9 to do violence to the name of God.
Prv 30:9 does not use the verb of the commandment in Ex 20:7; its verb denotes laying violent hold on something.
The sin feared in Prv 30:9 may be false swearing to deny a theft or an arraignment of God’s providence.
